title: Someone is scanning or probing your network
steps: Detect: note which device did the scanning and which devices and ports it looked at.
Analyse: if the scanner is one of your own devices, ask its owner whether a scan was planned (an IT check or a network tool). An unplanned scan from inside may mean that device is infected.
Respond: if the scanner is outside your network, make sure your router or firewall does not forward ports you do not need.
Respond: close or block any service that answered the scan and is not needed.
Recover: keep watching that device; a scan is often the first step before an attack.

title: Repeated login attempts (password guessing)
steps: Detect: note the service (for example SSH, RDP or FTP), the target device and where the attempts came from.
Analyse: check that device's login log for a successful login from the same address. Without one, there is no sign the guessing worked.
Respond: block the source address, and limit the service to the devices that really need it.
Respond: change weak or default passwords and turn on multi-factor login where possible.
Recover: if a login did succeed, treat the account as stolen: reset its password and look for changes made with it.

title: A device may be infected and talking to a control server
steps: Detect: note the device, the outside address or domain and how often it connected.
Analyse: check the outside address with a reputation service. Repeated, regular connections are a stronger sign than a single one.
Respond: disconnect the device from the network (unplug it or turn off Wi-Fi) but leave it powered on.
Respond: run an up-to-date antivirus scan; if malware is found or you are unsure, ask an IT professional or reinstall the system.
Recover: change passwords that were used on that device, from a different, clean device.

title: An attack attempt against a service or web application
steps: Detect: note the targeted device, the service or web address and the rule name or CVE.
Analyse: an attempt is not a success. Check whether the targeted software and version are affected, and look at the device's own logs around that time.
Respond: update the targeted software to a fixed version, or switch the service off if it is not needed.
Respond: if the service only needs to be reached from inside, block it from the Internet.
Recover: if there are signs it worked (new accounts, unknown programs, odd outbound traffic), isolate the device and get expert help.

title: Traffic that breaks a usual security policy
steps: Detect: note which device and which application or protocol was involved.
Analyse: ask whether this use is expected. Plain-text logins, file sharing or remote-access tools are often legitimate but risky.
Respond: if it is not wanted, remove the application or block it at the router.
Recover: if passwords were sent in plain text, change them and move to an encrypted alternative.

title: An attempt to overload a device or service (denial of service)
steps: Detect: note the target device or service and the volume and source of the traffic.
Analyse: check whether the service actually slowed down or stopped.
Respond: block the sources at the router; for large floods from the Internet, ask your Internet provider for help.
Recover: restart the affected service if needed and confirm it works again.

title: Suspicious traffic that is not clearly an attack
steps: Detect: note the devices involved and what made the traffic stand out.
Analyse: many of these alerts are harmless. Look for repeats over time or other alerts on the same device before acting.
Respond: if the device or outside address also appears in more serious incidents, follow that incident's guidance.
Recover: if it keeps happening and is harmless, note it so it is easier to recognise next time.

title: Data may be leaving the network
steps: Detect: note the device, the outside address and how much data was sent.
Analyse: check whether a backup, cloud sync or software update explains the transfer.
Respond: if not, disconnect the device and block the outside address.
Recover: find out what data was on the device and follow your legal or contractual duties if personal data may have leaked.
